correctness.rationale: After anchoring, variance is strictly convex; perturbing an untight connected component forces every maximizing tight-edge graph to span, hence all values are integral. The categorical product has diameter two. For three-level functions, exact variance is [N(s+t)-(s-t)^2]/N^2; all mutually row/column-compatible extreme sets are classified into a common line, singleton-versus-cross, or alternating 2-by-2 rectangle. Each category is optimized, checkerboard is bounded by the cross-star candidate, and elementary sign/monotonicity arguments give the full phase diagram including ties. Candidates are feasible. Independent exact enumerations on small grids and a large integer-phase comparison corroborate, but are not the proof.

evidence: Alon--Boppana--Spencer Theorem 2.1 yields integral optimizers on any graph, but not sharp values or equality families. Their Theorem 3.6 is for the sum metric, explicitly defined as a sum of factor distances.
Addario-Berry--Janson--McDiarmid arXiv:0902.1156 studies random graph models; its deterministic graph facts do not give this exact grid formula.
Yancey 2017 introduces Cartesian products via the sum of graph distances and studies variance optimality and concentration, not categorical products.
broader_coverage.reasoning: General graph integrality is an ingredient, not a broader quantitative bound implying our formula. The Cartesian product of cliques has the rook adjacency (one coordinate changes), whereas our edges require both to change. Earlier Kneser-pair graph calculations concern all two-subsets and cannot transfer sharp uniform-variance values to an induced cross-edge subgraph, whose vertex measure and constraints differ.

originality.rationale: Actual published search and accessible historical claims were compared by implications using categorical product, complement-rook, disjointness graph and induced Kneser aliases. The 1998 integral-extremizer theorem and Cartesian sum-product tensorization do not imply the all-parameter categorical three-envelope formula. The numerical 3-by-3 case is already obtainable by an isomorphism to the Cartesian product and is expressly not claimed separately as original. No broader exact classification identified; residual unindexed-equivalence risk remains.
residual_risks: No publication search can exhaust unindexed literature or inaccessible notes.
Indexed rook-graph summaries are not full-document inspections; their topics are not close to this spread invariant.
The 3-by-3 numerical special case follows from known Cartesian tensorization through an accidental isomorphism, but the full family does not.

value.rationale: This determines a natural Lipschitz-to-centered-L2 norm on an infinite family of connected categorical graph products, with a nontrivial exact transition among three qualitatively different optimizer geometries. It classifies every norming potential, all ties, and an exceptional checkerboard, beyond the known integrality principle; the distinction from Cartesian products makes the exact structure relevant to categorical metrics.
